catalog_quote: Djenne grammar sec. 3.1.2, pp.19-20: "Since syncope and accentual processes are rare in J-S of Djenné, there is not much to say about foot structure. CvCvCv words do not syncopate systematically to CvCCv, and tones do not behave as pitch-accent markers. There is no well-defined stress system as such. Stem-level tone melodies have a weak resemblance to pitch-accent, since there is rarely more than one H-toned peak on a stem. /LHL/ is a common lexical melody, but /HLH/ is rare in uncompounded stems ... However, stems of any size can be all-L-toned or all-H-toned; indeed, many entire nominal compounds surface as all-H or all-L due to Tone Leveling. This makes a pitch-accent analysis unattractive." || sec. 3.5, p.41: "In the absence of a weight-sensitive word-level accentual system, cliticization is of little phonological as opposed to morphosyntactic importance." || Cliffs grammar sec. 3.1.2, p.16: "There is no well-defined stress system as such. Stem-level tone melodies do not point to a pitch-accent system. Such a system would be more feasible in a two-level rather than three-level tone system. In addition, there is no requirement that a stem have exactly one tonal peak, as it would in a language with obligatory lexical accent. There are /L/-melodic stems, which have no tonal peak. /H/-melodic stems have stem-wide H-tone with no accented syllable. /MLH/-melodic stems have two separate tonal peaks (§3.6.1.4)."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jenaama is a lexical tone language (Djenné: H/L; Cliffs: H/M/L) with stem-level tone melodies; the grammarian states explicitly that there is no well-defined word-stress system and no weight-sensitive accentual system, and rejects a pitch accent analysis because stems may have zero or two tonal peaks.
new_statements.exceptions: Only a minor prosodic-weight effect: in Cliffs, light L-toned stems (Cv, Cvv, CvCv) become fully H under a floating H from the left while heavy stems (CvCvCv) take H only on the first syllable (sec. 3.6.3.1); in Djenné, stem weight conditions imperfective tone-dropping. No syllable is singled out as stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about word-internal (stem/word-level) metrical structure; clause-final intonation treated separately (sec. 2.1.5 / 3.7). Applies to both described varieties (Djenné Jenaama-Sorogaama and Cliffs Jenaama).
new_statements.identity_note: Heath's two 2022 grammars describe two varieties both filed under jena1242 by Glottolog: Jenaama-Sorogaama of Djenné (Pondori zone, the riverine 'core' Jenaama, 2 tone levels) and Cliffs Jenaama (pàālɛ̀-àmà, inland villages near Konna in the former 'Korondougou' group, 3 tone levels; Heath suggests it may merit separate-language status). Both grammars make the same no-stress statement. Lauschitzky 2007 / Wintoch 2000 describe the Djambakourou village dialect (2 tones). Monteil 1932 and Daget et al. 1953 mix several Bozo varieties (Djenné/Mopti Jenaama plus Tiéyaxo etc.).

tone.says: According to Heath 2025 sec. 2.1.2: 'Daget et al. (1953) had already stated that Bozo language (not yet differentiated into 4-5 languages) has three tone levels' but did not mark tones in the data ('from the pre-tonology era'). Heath adds that three levels is true of Tigemaxo and Cliffs Jenaama but not of Kelenga or Jenaama-Sorogaama of Djenné. The work itself was not opened in this task.
